title: Ad Creative Brief Template
description: Use this ad creative brief template to define your audience, offer, proof, format, and approvals before design or video production starts.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: A useful ad creative brief gives the designer or editor enough information to make a decision. Copy the fields below into your project document and fill them before production starts.

sections.title: The brief to copy
body: Campaign name: __. Business owner: __. Review owner: __. Due date: __. Primary outcome: __. Audience and buying situation: __. Offer and destination URL: __.
bullets: Message: the one thing the audience should understand.
Evidence: approved product facts, demonstrations or customer proof supporting that message.
Objection: the specific doubt this creative should answer.
Action: the next step and what happens after it.
Assets: logo, fonts, product images, footage, references and usage rights.
Deliverables: concepts, lengths, aspect ratios, languages and editable files required.

sections.title: An illustrative completed message
body: For a website service, the message might be “make it easier for customers to request a quote from their phone.” The evidence could be a real form demonstration; the action could be “review the project scope.” That is more usable than “make a viral premium ad.” Label any mockup as a concept and do not present invented customer results as proof.

sections.title: Agree review and testing rules
body: Specify included revision rounds and who provides one consolidated response. Define which variable each version changes: hook, demonstration, offer framing or visual treatment. Keep the destination and measurement ready before judging creative performance. Store the final approved brief beside the exports so the campaign operator can connect each file to its intended audience and test.

sections.title: Write the brief around a real decision
body: ‘Make it premium’ gives a designer little to work with. ‘Help a shop owner understand what is included in a one-page website’ names a reader and a decision. Add the question that currently stops that reader from enquiring: price, ownership, content requirements or uncertainty about the process.

Keep the main message to one sentence. Then list the facts available to support it. A screenshot can show a working form; it cannot prove that the form generated revenue. If proof is missing, change the claim or plan a clearly labelled demonstration rather than leaving the editor to invent evidence.

sections.title: A completed example for a service business
body: Illustrative brief: the audience is a small business owner with an outdated contact page. The message is that a clear mobile enquiry flow lets customers send the details needed for a quote. The asset is a screen recording using demonstration data. The action is to view the landing-page service and send an enquiry. No uplift percentage or client endorsement is claimed.

The production notes specify one vertical version and one square version, readable captions, the current logo and an end card using the approved contact route. The review owner checks service accuracy; the editor checks framing, audio and export quality. Stating those responsibilities prevents a design review from becoming a last-minute rewrite of the offer.

sections.title: Resolve missing inputs before the deadline
body: Mark each asset as supplied, to be created or awaiting permission. Name the person responsible and the date it is needed. A reference image is not automatically licensed artwork, and a draft testimonial is not permission to publish a customer’s words.

Agree how feedback will be collected. One consolidated response is easier to act on than conflicting messages from several people. Separate factual corrections from a new creative direction. If the brief changes after production starts, document which exports and timings are affected before continuing.

title: Facebook Ad Design Specs: A Production Checklist
description: Prepare Facebook and Instagram ad assets with a placement checklist covering aspect ratios, safe areas, copy, exports, and final account previews.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Plan Facebook and Instagram ad assets for their intended placements. Use aspect ratios as production starting points, then confirm the current requirements in Meta’s Ads Guide and account preview.

sections.title: Prepare a sensible export set
body: Common design canvases include square 1:1, portrait 4:5 and vertical 9:16. For example, a design team can prepare 1080×1080, 1080×1350 and 1080×1920 canvases. These are practical production sizes, not a claim that every placement accepts every format.
bullets: Keep key text, product details and the call to action clear of interface overlays.
Create a deliberate crop for each ratio instead of stretching the artwork.
Check small text and captions on an actual phone.
Review image rights, music permissions, spelling and destination consistency.

sections.title: Inspect the placement preview
body: Upload a draft and examine each planned placement in the account. Look for cropped faces, hidden subtitles, unreadable prices and missing brand context. Confirm file type, length, dimensions and other requirements in the current official guide before export approval. Platform specifications and supported formats can change.

sections.title: Give the operator an export manifest
body: Use filenames that identify concept, ratio, language and version. An example is quote-form-demo_9x16_en_v02.mp4. Include the approved copy, destination URL and notes about the intended placement. Retain the editable source separately from approved exports. A complete handoff reduces the chance that the right design is published with the wrong crop, old offer or mismatched caption.

sections.title: Design the crop instead of trusting an automatic resize
body: Start with the placements you intend to use. A square composition often needs more than extra background to become a vertical ad: the product, headline and call to action may need different positions. Keep a version for each intended ratio and inspect how the platform presents it.

Use the production canvases above as working examples, then confirm the live placement requirements before final export. File-size, duration and format limits can change. A file that uploads successfully can still have its key detail hidden behind a caption, button or interface overlay.

sections.title: Make a small-screen quality check
body: View the artwork at approximately the size a person will encounter it on a phone. Read the price and conditions without zooming. Check that thin text does not disappear over a busy photograph and that the product remains recognisable when cropped. Use sufficient contrast and avoid relying only on colour to communicate an important difference.

For video, inspect captions near the edges and review a few frames around every cut. A subtitle may be readable in the editing window but overlap a platform control after upload. Review the actual preview rather than assuming one safe-area template covers every placement.

sections.title: Keep exports easy to identify
body: A filename such as kitchen-demo_9x16_en_v03.mp4 tells the publisher more than final-final-new.mp4. Keep the concept, ratio, language and version consistent across the folder. Place approved files separately from working drafts and retain a brief note on the destination URL and copy.

Before handover, check spelling, product version, currency, price conditions, rights and the end card. Exporting an outdated offer accurately is still a publishing mistake. If the promotion ends on a real date, record that date so the campaign operator knows when the asset must be reviewed or retired.

title: Video Ad Script Template with an Example
description: Write a video ad as a sequence of decisions for the viewer. The script should connect an opening idea to a demonstration and a clear action, with each claim supported.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Write a video ad as a sequence of decisions for the viewer. The script should connect an opening idea to a demonstration and a clear action, with each claim supported.

sections.title: Copy this script structure
body: Audience: __. Problem or desire: __. Offer: __. Proof available: __. Main objection: __. Action: __.
bullets: Opening: a specific situation the intended customer recognises.
Demonstration: show what the offer does instead of relying on adjectives.
Explanation: connect the demonstration to a useful benefit.
Qualification: state an important limit or condition where needed.
Close: give one next step that matches the destination.

sections.title: Illustrative 20-second service script
body: Opening: “Do customers struggle to request a quote from your phone site?” Demonstration: show a short, labelled enquiry form being completed. Explanation: “A clear service page and working form make the next step easier.” Close: “Explore ReddyStack’s landing-page service.” The timing is a planning example; read it aloud and revise to suit the footage. It does not promise more leads or claim a client result.

sections.title: Review before recording
body: Check pronunciation, pacing, visible proof and whether the message works with captions. Remove unsupported superlatives, invented testimonials and urgency that is not real. Write a second opening only when it tests a different customer question. Keep the offer and main sequence stable if the purpose is to compare hooks. Approve the script before generating a presenter or editing every export size.

sections.title: Write what the camera can show
body: Separate spoken words from the visual instruction. ‘The service is easy’ is a claim; ‘show the customer choosing a service and receiving confirmation’ gives the production team a shot. If the action cannot be filmed or demonstrated accurately, rewrite the line before recording.

Read the script aloud at a comfortable pace. Do not squeeze an extra paragraph into the planned duration by making the voice unnaturally fast. Leave time to understand the demonstration and read important on-screen conditions. A short script with one clear idea usually creates fewer production problems than a list of every feature.

sections.title: Turn a vague line into a useful one
body: Vague: ‘Take your business to the next level with our amazing websites.’ More specific: ‘Show your services, explain what is included and let customers send a quote request from their phone.’ The second line gives the viewer something to evaluate and the editor something to show.

For a product, describe the actual action: a lid opening, a part fitting or a screen changing after a tap. Do not use generated footage that alters a product’s size, material or behaviour. An attractive shot that misrepresents the item creates a customer expectation the business cannot fulfil.

sections.title: Check the script against the destination
body: The final action should lead to the next step promised in the video. If the script says ‘see the full scope’, the link should make that scope easy to find. If it says ‘book’, confirm that booking is actually available rather than sending the viewer to an unrelated contact page.

Approve claims, pronunciation, names and required disclosures before recording multiple versions. Keep a script version number beside each export. When testing openings, preserve the body and destination where practical so the result can tell you something about the opening rather than an entirely different offer.

title: Ad Hook Examples for Clearer Creative
description: An ad hook should attract the people who might need the offer and give them a reason to continue. Attention that comes from a misleading promise can reduce lead quality.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: An ad hook should attract the people who might need the offer and give them a reason to continue. Attention that comes from a misleading promise can reduce lead quality.

sections.title: Five reusable approaches
body: These are original illustrative prompts, not proven winning ads. Replace the placeholders with accurate details from the business.
bullets: Recognisable task: “Still collecting website enquiries through three different channels?”
Demonstration first: “Here is what a customer sees after tapping Request a Quote.”
Objection: “What should you receive before approving a new landing page?”
Decision aid: “A business website or a campaign landing page: which fits this launch?”
Useful correction: “A cheap lead can still be expensive to turn into a customer.”

sections.title: Match the opening to the rest
body: A hook about cost should lead into a cost explanation. A demonstration hook should show the real workflow. For an illustrative product ad, “see how the lid opens with one hand” needs footage that actually demonstrates that action. Do not attract viewers with an unrelated sensational opening and then switch to the offer.

sections.title: Test the message fairly
body: Keep the body, audience and destination consistent when comparing openings. Review qualified actions and customer outcomes as well as early video engagement. A hook that increases views but attracts unsuitable people may weaken the campaign. Record what question each variant addresses and keep the finding in the next brief, rather than assuming the same opening works for every business.

sections.title: Choose the opening from the buyer’s question
body: Listen to the questions asked before someone buys. A website buyer may ask who writes the content, whether they keep the domain or what happens after launch. Those questions can produce useful openings because they describe a real uncertainty. ‘Here is what to prepare before your website quote’ attracts a different audience from a generic promise of instant growth.

Keep the scope honest. An opening about a complete cost breakdown needs a cost breakdown in the body. An opening about a product demonstration needs the actual product or a clearly identified demonstration. Curiosity becomes frustration when the rest of the ad never delivers the answer.

sections.title: Write variants that test different explanations
body: For an illustrative enquiry-page video, compare ‘Can a customer request a quote from your phone site?’ with ‘Three details your quote form should ask for.’ One starts with a problem; the other starts with a practical task. They offer a meaningful contrast while staying connected to the same service.

Changing only a synonym may produce little useful learning. Instead, label each variant by its idea: problem, demonstration, objection or decision aid. Keep the label in the asset register so you can recognise which approach was used when you review results weeks later.

sections.title: Look beyond the opening seconds
body: Early watch or click metrics can show whether the opening attracts attention, but suitable enquiries and purchases tell you whether it attracts useful attention. A sensational line may bring viewers who have no interest in the offer. Review the later stages before declaring it a winner.

Check comments and sales questions too. If people repeatedly misunderstand the price or think the ad is a job vacancy, the hook may need clearer qualification. Preserve the helpful parts of an opening and remove the misleading implication rather than simply making the next version louder.

title: An Ad Creative Testing Framework
description: Creative testing works best when each version answers a specific question. Decide what you want to learn before producing a large batch of nearly identical ads.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Creative testing works best when each version answers a specific question. Decide what you want to learn before producing a large batch of nearly identical ads.

sections.title: Write the hypothesis
body: Use a sentence such as “showing the mobile form before describing the service will help suitable buyers understand the offer.” Name the audience, outcome and competing version. Choose a platform experiment where available and appropriate; otherwise acknowledge that normal delivery differences limit a causal comparison.
bullets: Concept test: compare genuinely different message approaches.
Hook test: change the opening while retaining the body.
Proof test: compare relevant approved forms of evidence.
Format test: communicate the same offer with different media.

sections.title: Set a decision rule
body: Choose the primary business outcome and a review window that can accumulate useful results. Record spend and exposure per version. An illustrative test with two conversions in one version and one in another is weak evidence, especially if delivery was unequal. Avoid claiming statistical significance without an appropriate analysis and enough observations.

sections.title: Keep the learning usable
body: Record the creative ID, concept, offer, target, spend, outcomes and caveats. Move a successful concept into a controlled next test rather than changing five elements at once. Check whether an apparent winner has worse qualification or refund outcomes. Retire versions for a documented reason and preserve the source files so a later campaign can reuse the idea without recreating the whole production process.

sections.title: Keep a control you can explain
body: Save the existing version and describe why the new one might help. For example, a product demonstration may make an unfamiliar mechanism easier to understand than a lifestyle image. The test is about that explanation, not whether the editor prefers one visual style.

Record the audience, destination, offer, placements and dates. If the platform distributes impressions unevenly, acknowledge the limitation. A normal campaign comparison is not automatically a randomised experiment, and raw conversion counts do not account for unequal opportunity.

sections.title: Choose the outcome before seeing the result
body: A lead-generation test should define what counts as a suitable enquiry. An ecommerce test may need completed, non-test orders and later cancellation information. If you choose whichever metric looks best after the test, a weak asset can always be made to appear successful.

Avoid setting a universal number of days or conversions for every campaign. The useful sample depends on outcome frequency and the size of the difference you are trying to detect. With very little data, report a direction to investigate rather than a proven winner. A broken destination can justify stopping immediately; a small difference between working versions usually cannot.

sections.title: Keep the learning after the files are retired
body: Use a short record: hypothesis, asset IDs, spend, exposure, primary outcome, qualification or return outcomes, conclusion and next step. Include any changes made during the run. If the winning message depended on a seasonal offer, write that down before reusing it elsewhere.

A useful result can be negative. Discovering that buyers need to see the product size before they enquire may be more valuable than finding a slightly better background colour. Turn that finding into the next brief and keep the scope of the claim tied to the test that produced it.

title: Static vs Video Ads: Which Should You Test?
description: Static and video ads solve different communication problems. Choose the format that can explain the offer clearly with the assets and production time available.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Static and video ads solve different communication problems. Choose the format that can explain the offer clearly with the assets and production time available.

sections.title: Match format to the message
body: A static image can communicate a simple offer, product view or comparison quickly. Video can demonstrate a sequence, explain a process or show movement. Neither format has a universal performance advantage across businesses.
bullets: Use static when one frame can carry the essential decision information.
Use video when seeing the action helps explain the value.
Use a sequence or carousel when the message has distinct steps or options.
Account for the production effort needed to refresh and adapt the concept.

sections.title: Make a fair comparison
body: For an illustrative website offer, a static version could show the completed enquiry screen while a video shows the short journey to it. Keep the audience, promise and destination aligned, but adapt the execution to each medium. Comparing an unclear image with a polished demonstration does not isolate the value of the format itself.

sections.title: Judge business outcomes
body: Track relevant engagement, qualified enquiries or purchases and total production cost. Video views do not have the same meaning as completed enquiries; image clicks do not prove intent. Review whether the asset remains understandable on a phone and in the planned placements. Start with the strongest available concept, then use results to decide which format earns the next production investment.

sections.title: Ask what must be understood
body: A single image can show a product, a clear price condition or a simple choice. Video becomes useful when movement or sequence carries information: fitting a part, navigating a form or demonstrating how a feature behaves. Choose the medium after identifying that information.

Do not turn a clear static message into a video merely by animating every element. Motion can make the same message harder to read. Equally, a still frame may fail to explain an action that is easy to understand when seen once. The buyer’s question is a better starting point than a universal preference for either format.

sections.title: Include the cost of maintaining the asset
body: A business with frequent price or stock changes needs assets it can update accurately. Replacing text on a simple image may be quick; rerecording a presenter and rebuilding captions takes more work. That does not make video wrong, but it should affect the brief and budget.

Plan how each concept will adapt to the intended placements. A static layout and a video should each use their format well while presenting the same offer. Keep the promise and destination comparable instead of forcing identical execution into incompatible shapes.

sections.title: Use a fair business comparison
body: Suppose an illustrative video costs more to produce but explains the product well enough to reduce unsuitable enquiries. Its media cost per lead alone would miss part of the benefit. Conversely, an inexpensive static ad that produces suitable customers may be the better operating choice even if it earns fewer views.

Compare qualified outcomes, production effort and the time required for revisions. Keep audience, dates and exposure in the report. A single test supports a decision about that offer and context; it does not establish that one format always outperforms the other.

title: Creative Fatigue: Signs and a Response Plan
description: Spot possible creative fatigue by reviewing audience, frequency, offer, and conversion data. Plan a refresh based on evidence rather than one metric.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Creative fatigue is a possible explanation for declining ad response, not a diagnosis made from frequency alone. Check what changed in the audience, offer and buying journey before replacing every asset.

sections.title: Look for a pattern
body: Compare similar periods and inspect reach, frequency, response and business outcomes together. The same ad may still work for new viewers while becoming less useful to a repeatedly reached audience.
bullets: Response declines while exposure repeats within a comparable audience.
Qualified outcomes weaken without an obvious tracking or destination fault.
Comments reveal that the message is repetitive, unclear or no longer relevant.
The offer, stock or seasonal context has changed since the asset was produced.

sections.title: Rule out other causes
body: Illustrative example: conversion cost rises after a delivery fee increases, while ad engagement remains stable. That points toward the offer or checkout rather than automatically proving creative fatigue. A broken form, exhausted audience, measurement change or a promotion ending can produce similar headline trends. Diagnose the cause using the available evidence.

sections.title: Refresh the concept deliberately
body: Try a new objection, demonstration or message angle before only changing a background colour. Keep an effective control where practical and compare qualified outcomes. Maintain an asset register with concept, audience, first-use date and performance context. There is no universal frequency threshold or fixed weekly replacement schedule that fits every purchase cycle and campaign.

sections.title: Check the date the problem began
body: Place performance changes beside a dated log of offer, website and tracking changes. If conversion cost rose on the day shipping fees changed, investigate that connection before commissioning new creative. If reach stopped growing while repeat exposure increased, audience saturation may deserve attention.

Use comparable reporting periods and allow for normal variation. A quiet weekend or a few delayed sales can make a short window look worse. Keep the symptom separate from the diagnosis: ‘cost per qualified enquiry rose’ is observable; ‘the audience is bored’ needs supporting evidence.

sections.title: Refresh the unanswered question
body: Review sales conversations and comments for an objection the current ad does not address. A new demonstration, a clearer explanation of scope or an honest comparison may add useful information. Recolouring the same claim may make the file look new without giving the buyer a new reason to care.

Retain an effective control where practical. If the new version changes the offer, landing page and audience together, record that it is a broader campaign change rather than a clean creative-fatigue test. That distinction makes later learning more reliable.

sections.title: Manage a small, traceable asset library
body: Record the concept, audience, first-use date, offer version and intended placement for each asset. Mark why it was retired: inaccurate price, unavailable product, poor qualified outcomes or repeated exposure with weakening response. ‘Old’ is not a sufficient reason by itself.

Keep source files and rights information available. A useful concept can often be adapted to a new question without starting from scratch. Review frequency as context rather than applying one universal cutoff; a familiar low-cost purchase and a considered business service have different decision cycles.

title: Ad Copy Examples for Service Businesses
description: Good service-ad copy tells a suitable buyer what is offered and what to do next. These original examples are drafting starting points, not claims of campaign performance.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Good service-ad copy tells a suitable buyer what is offered and what to do next. These original examples are drafting starting points, not claims of campaign performance.

sections.title: Examples to adapt
body: Website service: “Give customers a clearer way to request a quote. Explore a landing page built around your offer, contact flow and mobile experience.”
Ad creative service: “Need a clearer campaign message? Plan ad images, video edits and copy around one offer and an agreed creative brief.”
Local SEO service: “Help customers understand where you work and what you offer. Review your website and eligible Google Business Profile information.”
AI presenter service: “Explain a product or service with an AI-presenter video. Start with an approved script, accurate assets and a clear next step.”

sections.title: Make each example true for the business
body: Replace broad nouns with the actual offer, audience and scope. Show evidence when available and include important conditions. If the service is remote, do not suggest a local office. If pricing is custom, do not advertise a fixed price that excludes essential work. A useful promise describes the deliverable without guaranteeing customers, revenue or rankings.

sections.title: Review and test
body: Read the copy together with the visual and destination. The three should make the same promise. Test a specific change such as clearer qualification or a different objection, then compare qualified outcomes. Avoid personal-attribute assumptions, fabricated testimonials and unsupported “number one” claims. Keep an approved copy sheet so edits made during publishing do not quietly change the agreed offer.

sections.title: Replace adjectives with information
body: ‘Premium’, ‘innovative’ and ‘best-in-class’ do not tell a buyer what they receive. Replace them with scope: a mobile-friendly service page, a tested enquiry form, three approved creative concepts or a report explaining completed work. Only use quantities that the actual proposal supports.

For an illustrative website offer, ‘A service page with your offer, key questions and a working contact route’ is more useful than ‘A stunning digital experience’. The first statement can be checked against the deliverable. It also makes a disagreement about scope easier to resolve before work starts.

sections.title: Use conditions where they affect the decision
body: A starting price needs a starting scope. A delivery promise needs the conditions that make it possible, such as approved content and timely feedback. A local claim needs a real service area. Put material conditions near the claim instead of hiding them on a distant page.

Write the copy and destination together. If the ad invites the reader to compare options, the page should explain those options. If it asks for a quote, describe the information needed. The transition should feel like continuing the same conversation.

sections.title: Edit for the person reading on a phone
body: Read the draft aloud. Remove phrases you would not use when explaining the service to a customer. Keep one main point per sentence and replace vague pronouns with the thing you mean. Check whether the text still makes sense beside the image and when shortened by the placement.

Before approval, inspect names, numbers, dates, links and evidence for claims. Keep an approved copy version with the asset. If a publisher changes the price or promise to fit a character limit, it needs another accuracy check. Concise wording is useful only while the meaning remains true.

title: Video Ad Storyboard Template
description: A storyboard connects the script to footage, on-screen text and production requirements. Use it to resolve missing assets before editing starts.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: A storyboard connects the script to footage, on-screen text and production requirements. Use it to resolve missing assets before editing starts.

sections.title: Copy the storyboard fields
body: Create one row per shot: shot number; approximate duration; visual or action; spoken line; on-screen text; audio; asset source; rights status; production note. Add a destination and end-card note at the top of the document.
bullets: Shot 1: introduce the customer situation with a recognisable visual.
Shot 2: demonstrate the relevant product or service action.
Shot 3: explain the decision information or answer an objection.
Shot 4: show the next step and accurate brand identity.

sections.title: An illustrative landing-page storyboard
body: Shot 1 shows a mobile visitor looking for contact information. Shot 2 shows the actual service page and enquiry fields. Shot 3 shows a clearly labelled test confirmation. Shot 4 invites the viewer to explore the service. Use demonstration data, not a real customer’s personal details. The example shows a workflow and does not claim an increase in conversions.

sections.title: Approve before production
body: Check that every shot has an available asset or a defined creation task. Confirm captions, safe areas and crop requirements for each placement. Record which elements may be AI generated and which must reproduce the real product accurately. Review the script, storyboard and claim evidence together so the editor does not have to invent proof or change the offer to fill a missing shot.

sections.title: Use the storyboard to expose missing evidence
body: For each shot, ask where the visual will come from. If the script says a product can perform an action, identify footage that shows the real action. If the only available material is a mockup, label it and keep the claim within what the mockup demonstrates.

A storyboard often reveals a weak script before production becomes expensive. ‘Show happy customers’ is not an available asset when there are no authorised customer images. Replace that shot with a product demonstration, an explanation or another piece of evidence the business actually has.

sections.title: Plan the sound and the silent version
body: Place the spoken line, caption and visual action beside each other. Check that the viewer has time to read the text while following the shot. Captions should preserve the meaning, including conditions and disclosures, rather than abbreviating the claim into something stronger.

Mark pauses and transitions where the information changes. Do not require the viewer to read a dense price card while listening to an unrelated sentence. Review whether the video remains understandable without sound and whether audio adds useful explanation when it is played.

sections.title: Approve a rough sequence before polished exports
body: A simple assembly of the planned shots can establish whether the sequence works. Review the offer, product accuracy, pacing and next step at that stage. Detailed animation and multiple aspect ratios can follow once those decisions are settled.

Keep a version number and record approvals. If a product photo or price changes, identify the affected shots and exports. The final check should compare the video with the approved script and destination, including the end card, captions, rights and any required disclosure. That is more dependable than judging the export only by whether it looks finished.

title: Ad Creative Performance Metrics
description: Read ad creative metrics across attention, clicks, and conversions. Use business outcomes and testing context to decide which assets to improve.
subtitle: Ad creative guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Creative metrics should help explain how a message contributes to business results. Read attention, response and conversion signals together instead of ranking assets by one engagement number.

sections.title: Use the right measurement layer
body: Start with the campaign objective and the action the creative asks for. A demonstration aimed at helping buyers understand a product serves a different role from a direct booking offer.
bullets: Attention: relevant video-start and watch measures, with their definitions stated.
Response: link clicks, landing-page visits and meaningful engagement.
Conversion: qualified enquiries or purchases linked to the agreed event.
Economics: media cost per useful outcome plus the production effort required.

sections.title: Compare like with like
body: An illustrative video may generate more views while a static offer produces more qualified enquiries. Neither is automatically the better asset without knowing the intended goal. Compare exposure, audience, placements, offer and period. A version that received most of the budget had more opportunity to accumulate results, so raw counts alone are a poor ranking method.

sections.title: Write a learning statement
body: Use “the product demonstration produced more qualified enquiries in this test” rather than “video always wins.” Record the supporting numbers and the limitations. Check for worse downstream outcomes, including unsuitable leads or returns. Keep the creative ID and message angle beside the results so the next brief can reuse a useful insight without confusing it with a universal rule.

sections.title: State exactly what a metric counts
body: Different video metrics can describe a start, a short view or a longer watch. Link clicks, all clicks and landing-page visits also answer different questions. Write the metric definition beside the number when comparing assets so the reader does not assume they are interchangeable.

Use rates with the relevant denominator and keep raw counts visible. Two conversions from very little exposure can look impressive as a rate while still providing weak evidence. An asset with more conversions may simply have received much more delivery.

sections.title: Connect attention to the next step
body: An opening can attract attention without helping a suitable buyer understand the offer. Review what happens after the click: did the page load, did the person submit, and was the enquiry useful? If the business receives questions unrelated to the service, the creative may be attracting the wrong expectation.

For ecommerce, include cancellations or returns when available. For services, include qualification and the sales response process. A persuasive asset should not create promises that the product or business cannot fulfil after the conversion.

sections.title: Keep a decision note with every comparison
body: Write the concept, audience, dates, spend, exposure and main outcome. Add what changed during the run and what remains uncertain. ‘The demonstration received more suitable enquiries in this test, but exposure was unequal’ is a more useful conclusion than calling it a universal winner.

Include production and revision effort when deciding what to make next. An expensive asset may be justified if it explains a difficult product well; a simple image may be sufficient for a clear offer. The purpose of reporting is to improve the next production decision, not to create a leaderboard of unrelated metrics.

title: AI UGC vs Human UGC: Choosing the Right Format
description: Compare AI UGC-style video and human UGC by use case, authenticity, cost, and production needs. Choose a format without misrepresenting real experience.
subtitle: AI UGC-style video guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: AI UGC-style video uses a synthetic presenter or generated production elements to resemble familiar social-video formats. Human UGC comes from a real person; the two should not be presented as interchangeable evidence.

sections.title: Compare what the viewer is being shown
body: A synthetic presenter can deliver an approved explanation. A real customer can describe an experience they actually had. An AI-presented script should not be framed as a customer testimonial or personal experience that never occurred.
bullets: AI presenter: useful for controlled scripts, explainers and planned versioning.
Human creator: useful when authentic use, personality or lived experience is central.
Product footage: valuable when viewers need to see the real item or workflow.
Hybrid: combine an accurately labelled presenter with genuine product demonstrations.

sections.title: Choose by the job
body: For an illustrative software explainer, a synthetic presenter can introduce a feature while actual screen recordings show it working. For an account of how a customer used a product, use a real authorised customer statement. Do not fabricate a person, review or before-and-after outcome to make an ad appear more credible.

sections.title: Plan approval and rights
body: Agree the script, voice, likeness permissions, source assets and disclosure approach before production. Confirm usage rights and how future edits will be handled. Review whether the final video could mislead someone about who is speaking or what has been demonstrated. Efficiency in production is useful only when the message remains accurate and suitable for the platform and target market.

sections.title: Decide whether the story needs lived experience
body: A person explaining the steps in a service can work from an approved script. A person describing how a product felt, fitted or changed their routine needs an actual experience to describe. That distinction should decide the presenter choice before appearance or production cost does.

For example, a synthetic presenter can introduce a screen recording of an appointment tool. It should not claim to have used the tool for months or recommend it as a customer. A human actor also should not be presented as a real customer when the story is fictional. The issue is the claim being made, not only the technology used to deliver it.

sections.title: Compare the production responsibilities
body: Human production needs briefing, scheduling, permissions and footage review. Synthetic production needs script approval, voice and likeness checks, generation review and clear labelling where required. Both need accurate product assets, editing and a final check against the offer. Neither route removes the need for editorial judgment.

A hybrid can be useful when a presenter explains the context while genuine footage demonstrates the product. Keep generated backgrounds or scenes separate from anything that a buyer could mistake for evidence of product performance. Document which elements are real and which are illustrative.

sections.title: Review what the viewer will reasonably believe
body: Watch the full video with its caption and landing page. Does the framing imply an independent review, a customer endorsement or a real event? If so, the underlying evidence and permissions need to support that interpretation. A small AI label cannot repair an invented success story.

Choose the route that communicates the offer accurately and can be maintained as the product changes. Measure suitable enquiries or purchases when the asset is used in a campaign. A lifelike presenter is a production characteristic, not proof that the message will persuade the right audience.

intro: A reliable AI-presenter workflow starts with the message and ends with a human review of the exported video. Generating a talking avatar is only one production step.

sections.title: Prepare the brief
body: Define the audience, offer, destination, length, language, presenter treatment and output formats. Use an approved script with accurate product facts. Collect brand assets and confirm that voice, likeness and other media can be used for the intended purpose.
bullets: Script review: wording, claims, pronunciation and an understandable next step.
Presenter setup: approved appearance, voice and consistent framing.
Production: short sections that can be corrected without regenerating the whole video.
Edit: actual product footage, captions and an accurate end card.

sections.title: Review a short sample first
body: Generate a sample containing the brand name, difficult words and any essential numbers. Check pronunciation, lip sync and whether the delivery suits the audience. Approving that sample before all versions can reduce avoidable rework. Avoid adding an unsupported claim just because the presenter makes it sound confident.

sections.title: Validate the final export
body: Watch the complete video at normal speed and inspect representative frames on a phone. Check captions against the approved script, verify numbers and test the destination link. Record the model or tool, source assets, approved version and agreed usage. Apply the disclosure approach appropriate to the content, platform and market, and keep real customer evidence separate from synthetic presentation.

sections.title: Lock the facts before generating the presenter
body: Create a short fact sheet containing the offer name, exact product version, price conditions, supported features and destination. Highlight anything still awaiting confirmation. The presenter should read an approved explanation, not fill gaps in the brief with plausible-sounding details.

Separate narration from production notes. Put pronunciation guidance beside names, abbreviations and amounts. If a sentence is hard to say naturally, shorten it. It is usually cheaper to repair an unclear sentence before generation than to hide awkward delivery with faster cuts.

sections.title: Approve a sample that tests the difficult parts
body: Include the brand name, a number, an unfamiliar term and a transition in the first sample. A generic greeting can look acceptable while the real script fails on the words that matter. Check speech, mouth movement, framing and whether the expression suits the subject.

Once approved, produce manageable sections and keep their filenames tied to the script version. This makes a correction to one sentence easier to trace. Retain the original approved sample as a reference, because individually acceptable clips can still feel inconsistent when assembled.

sections.title: Review the assembled video as a customer would
body: Watch the whole export at normal speed before inspecting individual frames. Check whether the explanation is understandable, captions are readable and the product footage supports the spoken claims. Then inspect tricky transitions, hands, text and packaging for visible errors.

Test the final destination and compare it with the end card. Save the script, asset permissions, review notes and export list together. When the offer changes, that record tells you which videos need updating. Publication is a separate check: apply the relevant platform’s current disclosure settings rather than assuming a production tool has handled them.

title: AI Product Demo Video Examples and Briefs
description: Explore original AI-assisted product demo concepts and briefs. Plan clear scripts and visuals without presenting unverified footage as a live product demonstration.
subtitle: AI UGC-style video guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: An AI-assisted product demo should make the real product easier to understand. The concepts below are original script and shot-list ideas to adapt, not published videos, client results or verified product demonstrations.

sections.title: Three illustrative demo concepts
body: Software: an AI presenter introduces a scheduling task, then a real screen recording shows the available booking flow. Use a test account and blur or replace personal details.
Physical product: a presenter explains one feature while actual footage shows the item in use. Keep dimensions, labels, colours and included accessories accurate.
Digital service: a presenter outlines the delivery steps while approved diagrams or screen captures show the agreed process. Do not invent a dashboard or result that the service does not provide.

sections.title: Write the demo brief
body: Record the user task, starting state, required actions and ending state. Identify which shots must be real and which can be illustrative. Provide the product version and reference assets so the editor can check continuity. If a concept visual is used, label it clearly and avoid presenting an imagined feature as available.

sections.title: Review against the product
body: Ask someone who knows the product to compare the video with the actual experience. Test every shown step, confirm the current offer and remove unsupported performance claims. Check that the final call to action lands on a matching page. A polished demonstration that changes the shape, interface or behaviour of the product can create more confusion than a simpler accurate recording.

sections.title: Show a task with a beginning and an end
body: A software demonstration should identify the starting state, the user’s action and the result. For a booking tool, that might be selecting an available time and receiving confirmation in a test account. Show enough context for the viewer to understand what changed rather than cutting between unrelated attractive screens.

A physical-product demonstration needs the same discipline. Show the actual item, the relevant movement and any condition that affects the result. Do not let generated footage invent an accessory, change the packaging or imply that the product performs a task it cannot perform.

sections.title: Use a shot list with accuracy checks
body: For each shot, record the source, product version and claim it supports. A real screen capture can demonstrate an existing feature. A concept animation can explain an idea if clearly identified, but should not masquerade as an available interface. Keep personal data out of recordings by using an appropriate demonstration account.

Ask the person responsible for the product to review the sequence. Can they repeat the shown steps? Are any important limitations omitted? If the demonstration skips a waiting period or approval step, make sure the edit does not promise an instant outcome the product does not deliver.

sections.title: Give the viewer the next piece of information
body: The final link should lead to the demonstrated product or service, with the relevant specifications, scope or enquiry route. Sending a viewer to a generic homepage can force them to start the search again. Keep the wording consistent across the video and destination.

A useful demo can be simple: one task, genuine footage and a clear explanation. Review viewer questions after publication to identify missing information for the next version. Do not interpret a visually convincing clip as proof of increased sales until a properly defined campaign or product test provides that evidence.

intro: An AI video script should be written for spoken delivery and checked against real evidence. Approve the wording before generation so the presenter does not become the first place an unclear offer is discovered.

sections.title: Copy the production template
body: Audience: __. Business goal: __. Offer: __. Approved proof: __. Presenter type: __. Language and pronunciation notes: __. Disclosure treatment: __. Destination: __.

Main explanation: explain one useful part of the offer in plain language.
Demonstration cue: name the real footage or visual that supports it.
Important condition: state any limit needed to understand the offer.
Final line: give one accurate next step.

sections.title: Illustrative service script
body: “Planning a new business website? Start by deciding what a visitor should do next. Your pages, mobile layout and enquiry form should support that action. Explore ReddyStack’s website-development service to discuss the scope.” Pair the line with real page or form examples where available. It explains an approach without impersonating a customer or promising a result.

sections.title: Make generation easier to review
body: Use short sentences and spell out ambiguous numbers in the pronunciation notes. Mark pauses and visuals separately from spoken copy. Generate a sample with the most difficult words before the full version. Compare the completed captions and narration with the approved script, including the final offer and destination. Synthetic delivery should never be used to invent an endorsement or personal experience.

sections.title: Write for a voice, not a brochure
body: Read each line aloud and remove the phrases you would not use in a conversation. ‘We offer comprehensive solutions’ can become a concrete description of the work. Short sentences help with pronunciation, captions and later corrections, but the script should still sound like one connected explanation.

Keep difficult words and numbers in a pronunciation note. Write exactly what the audience should hear, including the currency or unit when it matters. A generated voice can sound confident while saying a product name incorrectly, so fluency alone is not an approval test.

sections.title: Pair every important line with evidence
body: If the script says customers can submit a request from their phone, show that flow using demonstration data. If it describes a deliverable, show an accurate example or explain the scope. Avoid a presenter saying ‘I tried this’ unless the content is genuinely a permitted account of that person’s experience.

Mark any sentence that depends on a price, deadline or performance claim. Check it with the business before production. Remove claims that cannot be supported instead of hoping the final disclosure will make them acceptable.

sections.title: Make approval easy to repeat
body: Use one document with columns for narration, visual, caption, pronunciation and review status. Approve the message before ordering multiple languages and aspect ratios. A small script change can affect speech length, lip sync, captions and every export.

At the end, compare the delivered video with the approved text line by line. Listen for omitted conditions, changed numbers or an incorrect call to action. Check the placement preview as well as the source file. Keep the final script version with the export so later updates begin from the wording that was actually published.

title: AI UGC-Style Video Cost: Scope the Quote
description: Scope AI UGC-style video costs across concepts, generation, editing, revisions, and formats. Compare quotes against the deliverables you need.

intro: AI UGC-style video pricing depends on the production scope, not only the final video length. A useful quote separates concept work, generation, editing and the versions you need to publish.

sections.title: List the cost drivers
body: Ask what is included before comparing two prices. A single approved script in one format is a different job from several concepts, languages and placement versions.
bullets: Concept and copy: research, scripts and claim review.
Generation: presenter, voice, attempts and tool usage.
Editing: real footage, motion, captions, sound and end card.
Variants: hooks, languages, durations and aspect ratios.
Rights and handoff: permitted usage, project files and revision scope.

sections.title: Count the actual deliverables
body: Illustrative scope: two concepts with two hooks each and two aspect ratios can produce eight exports. That does not necessarily require eight completely independent edits, but each export still needs checking. Ask which changes are included and which reopen script or production approval. Avoid treating “unlimited revisions” as meaningful unless its boundaries are clear.

sections.title: Compare the total usable outcome
body: Request a sample, a deliverable list, the review process and any recurring tool costs. State who supplies product footage and who verifies pronunciation and claims. ReddyStack quotes work against an agreed scope; this guide does not publish a fixed market rate or guaranteed turnaround. A lower generation cost is not a saving if inaccurate or unusable exports require the entire video to be remade.

sections.title: Count concepts separately from exports
body: A concept is a distinct message or demonstration. An export is a delivered file in a particular format. One concept adapted to three aspect ratios is not the same workload as three independently scripted concepts, even though both may produce three files. Ask a supplier to make that distinction in the quote.

Languages, hooks and durations can multiply the review work. Each version needs accurate speech, captions, framing and an end card. Shared source material can reduce production effort, but it does not eliminate the need to inspect the finished variants.

sections.title: Identify the inputs that could cause rework
body: Common missing inputs include approved product footage, pronunciation guidance, usage permissions and a settled offer. If those arrive after generation, the presenter, edit and captions may all need changing. A cheaper initial quote can become expensive when it assumes the customer will supply work that has not been prepared.

Agree the review stages: script, presenter sample, rough edit and final exports. State which corrections are included and which changes reopen an approved stage. A factual error introduced during production is different from a customer changing the offer after approving the script.

sections.title: Compare what you can actually publish
body: Request a deliverable list that includes concept count, languages, ratios, approximate lengths, source-file arrangements and usage rights. Confirm whether tool subscriptions or asset licences continue after delivery and who is responsible for them. Do not assume every generated asset can be used in every market or placement.

ReddyStack prices this work after the scope is clear. There is no fixed market price in this guide because the production requirements vary. Judge the proposal by the accurate, approved files it will deliver and the work required to maintain them, rather than the cost of one generation attempt.

sections.title: Create the reference pack
body: Use the approved logo, colour values, fonts, product images, voice notes and example frames. Record presenter treatment, pronunciation, caption style and the terms the business uses for its offers. A vague request to “match the brand” leaves too many decisions open.
bullets: Identity: correct brand name, logo and product terminology.
Visuals: consistent framing, backgrounds and accurate product details.
Voice: approved pronunciation, tone and pace.
Message: matching offer, qualifications and call to action.
Rights: permission for assets, voices and likenesses across planned uses.

sections.title: Use a continuity review
body: For an illustrative product series, compare clips side by side: does the packaging change, does a logo distort, or does the presenter’s voice shift? Build short reference frames for reviewers instead of relying on memory. Regenerate only the affected segment when the rest is correct, then review the assembled export again.

sections.title: Keep a version record
body: Store the approved script, settings, source assets and final exports under one project version. Lock the core reference pack before translating or resizing, while allowing deliberate adaptations for each audience. Do not force identical pacing into every language if it harms understanding. Brand consistency means recognisable and accurate communication, not preserving an error across every video.

sections.title: Create a small reference pack people can use
body: Include the approved logo files, colour values, fonts, product images and examples of acceptable framing. Add how the brand name is pronounced and how the offer should be described. A folder of dozens of unrelated inspiration images can be less useful than a few clear references with notes.

Identify what must remain exact. Product labels, packaging, interface text and price conditions are factual details. Background mood and camera framing may allow more interpretation. Make that distinction explicit so a visually attractive generation is not approved while quietly changing the product.

sections.title: Compare neighbouring clips together
body: A presenter’s voice or appearance can shift between individually generated segments. Packaging may change shape or text may become distorted. Put the clips side by side and compare them with the reference frames instead of relying on memory.

Review the transitions in the assembled edit. A small difference that is hard to notice in isolation may be obvious at a cut. Fix the affected segment and then check the complete sequence again, including captions and audio levels. A local repair can create a new continuity problem elsewhere.

sections.title: Keep the approved message attached to the files
body: Use a version record for the script, source assets and exports. If the offer changes, identify every language and ratio that contains the old wording. This is particularly important when one team generates the presenter and another adds captions or publishes the ad.

Consistency should make the business recognisable and the offer accurate. Allow deliberate adjustments for the medium and language. Forcing the same sentence length or crop into every version can harm clarity even when the colours and logo match perfectly.

title: AI UGC-Style Video Disclosure: A Review Checklist
description: Review AI UGC-style video disclosures, synthetic presenters, and commercial relationships. Use this checklist alongside current platform and local rules.
subtitle: AI UGC-style video guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Disclosure should help viewers understand synthetic presentation and commercial relationships. The right treatment depends on the content, platform and target jurisdiction, so review current rules before publishing.

sections.title: Separate three questions
body: Is the presenter or scene synthetic? Is the message an advertisement or sponsored endorsement? Does the content imply a real person had an experience? These questions can require different explanations; one small “AI” label does not automatically resolve all of them.
bullets: Do not invent a customer review or present a synthetic speaker as a satisfied customer.
Do not imply a person endorsed the offer without permission.
Identify commercial relationships where applicable.
Use an appropriate platform label and understandable disclosure when required.

sections.title: Review what an ordinary viewer would infer
body: An illustrative AI presenter explaining a website service can be described as an AI presenter. A script saying “I bought this and doubled my sales” creates a purported personal experience and result that need real evidence; labelling the speaker AI does not make a fabricated claim true. Check the complete video, caption, landing page and visual context together.

sections.title: Keep evidence with the project
body: Record asset and likeness permissions, approved claims, the publication market and the disclosure decision. The FTC’s endorsement resources explain relevant US advertising principles; other countries and platforms have their own requirements. This checklist is a production review aid, not a determination that a particular advertisement complies with every applicable law. Obtain qualified advice for uncertain or regulated claims before publication.

sections.title: Describe the content plainly
body: Use wording the viewer can understand, such as ‘AI presenter’ when that accurately describes the speaker. Keep the explanation connected to the part of the video that could be misunderstood. A vague production credit may not explain that a realistic speaker is synthetic.

Separate a presenter from an endorsement. A scripted explanation of a product is different from a customer saying it solved a personal problem. If the story did not happen, remove the testimonial framing. Changing the face or adding an AI label does not turn a fictional experience into evidence.

sections.title: Check the destination platform before publication
body: YouTube provides an altered-content disclosure process for relevant realistic synthetic or altered material. Its current guidance should be checked for the actual video being uploaded. Other platforms and advertising products have their own rules and may display their own labels. A label applied in one place does not settle the requirements everywhere the file is reused.

Record the intended platforms and markets in the brief. If the same clip will appear as an organic post and a paid advertisement, review both uses. Keep the caption, landing page and commercial relationship consistent with what the video communicates.

sections.title: Keep an approval record without overstating it
body: Store the approved script, the source of each claim, permissions for voices and likenesses, and the disclosure decision. Name the person responsible for checking the final publication settings. A production checklist supports review; it is not a certificate that the advertisement meets every applicable rule.

If the video makes uncertain health, financial or other regulated claims, obtain an appropriate specialist review before publication. For an ordinary service explainer, the practical starting point is simpler: show what is real, identify synthetic presentation where needed and remove statements that the business cannot substantiate.

title: AI Video Localization Checklist

intro: Localizing an AI video means adapting its meaning and offer for the intended audience. Translation alone does not resolve differences in pronunciation, pricing, delivery or customer expectations.

sections.title: Prepare the market brief
body: Name the language, region, audience and reviewing person. Confirm that the promoted service is actually available in that market and that the destination page supports the same promise.
bullets: Language: terminology, idiom and names reviewed by a competent speaker.
Numbers: dates, currency, units and spoken amounts checked.
Offer: availability, delivery and important conditions match the market.
Visuals: captions and on-screen text fit after translation.
Rights: voice and media permissions cover the intended region and use.

sections.title: Test a difficult passage first
body: Use a short sample containing the brand name, a price, a location and the main call to action. Have the reviewer check pronunciation and meaning, not only whether the voice sounds fluent. An illustrative English script may need fewer spoken points in another language to remain comfortable at the same duration; rewriting can be better than accelerating the voice.

sections.title: Check every final variant
body: Review audio and captions together on a phone. Confirm the destination URL, contact process and local offer details. Keep a version matrix by language and aspect ratio so outdated captions are not paired with new narration. Use the same approved source message, but allow genuine linguistic adaptation. Never claim native-language support or local offices that the business cannot actually provide.

sections.title: Translate the intended action
body: Begin with what the viewer should understand and do. A literal translation may preserve the words while changing the tone or making the next step unclear. Ask a competent reviewer to check the message in context, including the page the viewer will visit.

Check practical details: currency, units, dates, service availability and contact options. A fluent voice advertising a service unavailable in that market is still an inaccurate video. Do not imply local support, a staffed office or a language capability that the business cannot provide.

sections.title: Make room for the translated sentence
body: Some versions need more space or time than the source language. Rework the sentence or shot timing rather than compressing the voice until it sounds unnatural. Check that captions remain readable and that the spoken offer has not lost an important condition.

Test the hardest passage first: brand name, place name, price and call to action. Ask the reviewer what they understood, not only whether the accent sounds acceptable. A small pronunciation error can change a name or number that is central to the offer.

sections.title: Track every version through approval
body: Maintain a matrix of language, ratio, script version, caption version and review status. When the source offer changes, update every affected variant. This prevents an old translation from being paired with new footage or a corrected voice track from shipping with outdated captions.

Review the final export on a phone with sound on and off. Confirm that the destination page, form and response process can serve that audience. Save the approved translation and reviewer notes with the asset so the next update does not depend on somebody remembering why a phrase was chosen.

title: AI Video Quality Checklist Before Publishing
description: Review the final AI-assisted video as an advertisement a customer will see. Technical export success is not the same as an accurate, understandable and publishable asset.

intro: Review the final AI-assisted video as an advertisement a customer will see. Technical export success is not the same as an accurate, understandable and publishable asset.

sections.title: Inspect content and continuity
body: Watch the whole export at normal speed first. Then inspect difficult frames and transitions where generation or editing errors are more likely to be visible.
bullets: Product: labels, shape, accessories and demonstrated behaviour remain accurate.
Presenter: facial movement, hands, gaze and voice are acceptable for the intended use.
Text: brand names, captions, prices and conditions match the approved script.
Audio: speech is intelligible and music does not obscure key words.
Edit: transitions, pacing and crops preserve the meaning.
Disclosure and rights: required labels and permissions are in place.

sections.title: Test the actual viewing context
body: Open the file on a phone, with sound on and off, and review the intended placement preview. Check whether interface elements cover captions or the call to action. sections.title: Define acceptance and rework
body: Record each issue by timestamp, expected result and required correction. Fix the affected segment, then watch the complete replacement export to catch new problems. Keep the approved version and distribution list together. Avoid publishing first and treating viewer complaints as quality assurance, especially when a video shows product capabilities or customer claims.

sections.title: Check the message before the pixels
body: Watch once without stopping and explain what the offer is. If the answer is unclear, polishing individual frames will not solve the main problem. Confirm the audience, product, important conditions and next action before examining generation artefacts.

Then compare the narration and captions with the approved script. Look for changed numbers, missing negatives, incorrect names and conditions lost in a shortened caption. Those errors can materially alter the promise even when the video looks professional.

sections.title: Use two review passes
body: The first pass follows the customer experience: clarity, pacing, sound, captions and destination. The second examines accuracy and continuity: product shape, labels, hands, interface text, transitions and the match between shots. Record issues by timestamp so the editor can reproduce them.

Test the intended viewing size and placement preview. Captions should convey the speech and relevant audio information, and important text should remain readable without zooming. Do not let music or sound effects cover the words that explain the offer.

sections.title: Verify the replacement export
body: After a correction, review the full replacement rather than checking only the repaired frame. Regeneration can introduce a different voice, changed product detail or new spelling error. Confirm the version number and remove ambiguity about which file is approved for publication.

Keep the issue list, final script, rights information and export manifest together. If a price, product or policy changes later, this record helps identify what needs replacing. The acceptance decision should be based on accurate, usable content, not on how many attempts were spent creating it.

body: Opening: “What happens after you send an enquiry?” Body: explain the real review, scope and approval steps. Close: invite a suitable buyer to explore the service. This can be useful for a service business when uncertainty about the process stops people taking the next step.

sections.title: Turn a concept into a production brief
body: Choose one audience, one message and one action. Provide approved facts, footage, presenter requirements, caption language and disclosure treatment. Review a sample and test the destination before launch. Compare qualified outcomes across concepts rather than assuming the most lifelike presenter will perform best. Never add a fabricated first-person customer story to make the concept appear more authentic.

sections.title: Example: explain a service without inventing a customer
body: A presenter opens with ‘What happens after you request a website quote?’ The next shots show a demonstration brief, a page list and a review checklist. The presenter explains that scope, content responsibilities and approval points are agreed before work starts. The end card links to the relevant service page.

This concept uses the business’s process as the subject. It does not need a synthetic person pretending to be a satisfied customer. Use demonstration documents with no private details and keep the steps consistent with what the business actually offers.

sections.title: Example: let the real product do the demonstrating
body: For an illustrative appointment tool, the presenter names the task and a real screen recording shows a test booking from selection to confirmation. The narration explains what the viewer sees. If the feature requires a particular plan or setup, include that condition where it affects the buying decision.

Keep generated scenes away from factual product behaviour. A concept animation can introduce an idea, but it should not invent an available dashboard or make a slow process appear instant. Have someone familiar with the product repeat the shown steps before approving the edit.

sections.title: Choose a concept you can support with assets
body: List the footage, facts and permissions available today. A modest explanation with accurate screen captures is often more usable than an ambitious story built on assets that do not exist. Write the script around one customer question and one next action.

When the concept is tested, compare suitable enquiries or purchases with the intended goal and keep production cost visible. These examples are production starting points, not proven winning advertisements. The useful lesson comes from how a clearly defined audience responds to an accurate offer in a measured test.

intro: A website brief should connect the business goal to the pages, content and actions that must work at launch. Copy this checklist into a shared document before requesting a quote.

sections.title: Define the job
body: Business and contact owner: __. Main audience: __. Primary offer: __. Launch goal: __. Primary visitor action: __. Decision maker: __. Desired date and reason: __. Budget range: __.
bullets: Pages: list each page and the question it answers.
Content: identify who supplies copy, images, product data and permissions.
Functionality: forms, payments, bookings or integrations with clear acceptance criteria.
SEO: existing URLs to retain, priority topics and redirect requirements.
Operations: domain, hosting, business email, analytics and access ownership.
Handoff: editing needs, documentation and support after launch.

sections.title: An illustrative acceptance criterion
body: “The enquiry form works” is incomplete. A stronger brief says: “A mobile visitor can submit a valid enquiry, sees confirmation, and the assigned business mailbox receives one message; invalid submissions show clear field errors.” Define equivalent checks for checkout, search or booking if they are in scope.

sections.title: Separate essential work from later ideas
body: Mark each requirement as launch-critical or a later improvement and state what is explicitly excluded. Agree revision rounds, feedback timing and who approves production. Keep existing search-performing pages and business integrations visible in the brief so redesign work does not accidentally remove them. A clear scope improves the usefulness of quotes and gives both sides a shared way to decide whether the website is ready.

sections.title: Give each page a job
body: Write a page list with the question each page answers. The homepage introduces the offer; a service page explains fit and scope; a project page shows work that can be inspected; the contact page helps a suitable person take the next step. If two proposed pages answer the same question with almost the same content, reconsider whether both are needed.

List existing URLs beside the new plan. Mark pages that already receive enquiries, search traffic or external links. A redesign brief that ignores those pages can accidentally replace useful content with a visually cleaner but less informative site.

sections.title: Describe behaviour with examples
body: For an enquiry form, specify the required fields, success message, recipient and failure behaviour. For a booking system, explain availability, cancellation and double-booking rules. For a store, describe products, variants, shipping and failed payments. These examples expose requirements that ‘add a form’ or ‘build ecommerce’ leaves unclear.

Include what should not happen. An invalid submission should not create a lead event; a user should not see another customer’s data; a failed payment should not look like a confirmed order. The brief does not need implementation jargon to state these boundaries clearly.

sections.title: Prepare the handover before the build
body: Identify who owns the domain, hosting, email and third-party accounts. Give the developer appropriate access rather than transferring ownership casually. Decide who will edit content after launch and what instructions they need.

Keep launch-critical work separate from later ideas, with a reason for each priority. Agree one review owner, revision rounds and the date by which content must be supplied. A useful brief leaves fewer decisions hidden inside the quote and gives both sides a concrete way to check the finished website.
