title: Business Website Launch Checklist
description: Use this business website launch checklist to review mobile usability, forms, content, search setup, security, and ownership before going live.
subtitle: Website development guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: A launch checklist should test the website as a customer and as the person who operates it. Complete these checks on the actual production domain before treating the launch as finished.

sections.title: Check the customer journey
body: Read the offer and click the main navigation from a phone and desktop. Complete the primary action with clearly marked test data. Confirm the business received it and can respond.
bullets: Content: correct identity, services, contact details and approved proof.
Forms: labels, validation, delivery, confirmation and duplicate handling.
Commerce or booking: successful and failed flows where included.
Accessibility: keyboard operation, visible focus and readable text.
Performance: sensible image sizes and usable loading on a slower connection.

sections.title: Check search and operations
body: Confirm important pages return successful responses, use their intended canonical URLs and are not accidentally marked noindex. Validate the sitemap and robots file. Test any redirects from changed URLs and check internal links for old destinations. Confirm HTTPS, domain ownership, analytics configuration and access for the people who maintain the site.

sections.title: Leave a launch record
body: Record the deployed version, checks performed, known limitations and rollback approach. Make one real production smoke test after deployment; a local preview is not proof that production forms and environment settings work. Check Search Console for discovery and indexing signals over time. Submitting a sitemap helps discovery but does not guarantee that every page will be indexed or ranked. Assign an owner for enquiries and future maintenance.

sections.title: Test the routes a customer actually uses
body: Start from a service link, a shared article and the homepage rather than always entering through the same page. Open the menu, read the offer, use the main contact action and return with the browser’s back button. Check the same journey on a phone with the keyboard open.

Use clearly labelled test information for the enquiry. Verify delivery to the intended business destination, not only the success message on screen. Also test invalid input and a temporary delivery failure. The visitor should receive a useful error and retain the information needed to try again.

sections.title: Check production-specific settings
body: A preview may have different credentials, allowed domains or environment settings. Confirm the production domain, HTTPS, form delivery and intended analytics property after deployment. Check that a preview-only noindex setting or access restriction has not reached the public pages.

Inspect representative pages directly: homepage, service detail, article, project and contact. Verify the expected title, canonical URL and visible content. Test old links if URLs changed. A sitemap listing a page does not prove that its content loads or that Google has indexed it.

sections.title: Leave a usable launch record
body: Record the deployed version, checks completed, any unresolved limitations and the person responsible for follow-up. Keep a recovery route if a material issue appears. Include account ownership and renewal responsibilities so a domain or tool does not later expire unnoticed.

After launch, review actual enquiry delivery and Search Console signals. Separate ordinary reporting delays from reproducible faults. When a problem is found, record the affected URL, device and steps to reproduce it. ‘The site feels broken’ is difficult to act on; a specific failed journey can be repaired and retested.

intro: An ecommerce website quote should describe the store the business needs to operate. Product complexity, checkout, integrations and ongoing responsibilities usually explain the price better than page count alone.

sections.title: List the build and running costs
body: Separate one-time implementation from recurring platform and operating costs. Ask which items are supplied by the business and which are part of the developer’s scope.
bullets: Store setup: design, templates, navigation and essential content.
Catalogue: number of products, variants, data cleanup and import work.
Checkout: payments, shipping logic and applicable business requirements.
Integrations: inventory, order processing, email or other agreed systems.
Operations: hosting or platform plan, domain, extensions and support.

sections.title: Use a quote comparison worksheet
body: For each proposal, write the included product count, template scope, revision rounds, migration work, payment setup and acceptance tests. Add twelve months of known recurring fees to understand the first-year commitment. A hypothetical store with 30 simple products and manual fulfilment is a different scope from a catalogue with thousands of variants and inventory synchronisation. This comparison is not a market-rate estimate or a fixed ReddyStack price.

sections.title: Agree acceptance and ownership
body: Test a real checkout path, failed payment, stock change, shipping calculation and order confirmation. Confirm who owns the accounts and who can update products after handoff. Clarify support boundaries and the cost of later changes. Avoid selecting solely on the cheapest build quote when essential catalogue preparation, recurring tools or operational checks are omitted. Ask for a scoped proposal against your actual store requirements.

sections.title: Catalogue preparation can change the quote
body: Thirty products with one image and one price each are different from thirty products with sizes, colours, variant stock and separate delivery conditions. Count variants and required data fields before requesting estimates. Missing descriptions, inconsistent SKUs and unlicensed images create work even when the store platform is already chosen.

Prepare a sample of representative products, including the most complicated one. Ask how imports, updates and discontinued items will be handled. A cheap initial setup can become difficult to maintain if every routine change requires a developer.

sections.title: Write down the operational exceptions
body: Describe what happens when stock changes during checkout, a payment fails, a customer requests cancellation or an order needs a refund. Specify shipping areas, charges and any restrictions the business actually applies. These rules affect both development scope and the information customers need before buying.

Check the accounts and integrations required to fulfil an order. Payment, inventory, shipping and email services can each introduce recurring charges and access requirements. Compare the first-year commitment using current vendor quotes rather than assuming the build price covers every operating cost.

sections.title: Compare acceptance criteria, not screenshots
body: A proposal should explain how a completed order, failed payment, inventory update and customer notification will be checked. Confirm who supplies product data and policies and who approves them. Do not allow a sample storefront’s return terms to become the business’s policy by accident.

Keep ownership and support explicit. Who controls the domain and store account? Who can change product information? What is covered after launch, and what is a separately priced improvement? ReddyStack provides a scoped quote because a store’s operational requirements matter more than a generic page count.

sections.title: Separate the deliverables

bullets: Offer and copy: audience, value, objections and action.
Design: original composition or adaptation of an existing system.

Their prices cannot be compared as if they purchase the same work. List the missing tasks, assign an owner and include any recurring tools in the decision. This guide deliberately uses scope examples rather than unsupported market-average prices.

sections.title: Define success before work begins
body: Write the acceptance criteria: the mobile page is usable, the offer is accurate, a valid enquiry reaches the business and tracking records the intended action once. Confirm the number of variants, included revisions and post-launch support. A landing page cannot guarantee a conversion rate independently of traffic quality, offer, pricing and response handling. Choose a provider using the deliverables and review process as well as the quote.

sections.title: A one-page site can still contain substantial work
body: Page count is a poor shortcut for effort. A single page may require offer research, original copy, product photography, responsive design, a lead integration and measurement. Another may be a straightforward adaptation of an existing design with supplied content. List those tasks before comparing quotes.

Decide what the visitor should do and what information they need first. A quote-request page needs scope and qualification; a product launch may need demonstrations and delivery details. The content problem should shape the page rather than being added after the layout is finished.

sections.title: Clarify who supplies the missing pieces
body: Ask who writes the copy, prepares images, checks claims and owns the domain. Identify the form recipient and any CRM or booking integration. If a tool charges monthly, show that separately from the build. If multiple ad variants need distinct pages, count the variants explicitly.

Agree review points before production. Changing the offer after copy and design approval can require more than editing a headline. Define included revisions and distinguish factual corrections from a new direction. A clear scope is more valuable than an attractive headline price with undefined exclusions.

sections.title: Define what delivery means
body: The page should work at the intended mobile sizes, send a valid enquiry to the right destination and handle errors understandably. Titles, metadata, canonical URL and measurement should match the agreed use. Check the live deployment after the preview is approved.

A provider can deliver and verify the page, but cannot guarantee a conversion rate independently of traffic, price, trust and response handling. Use the first campaign results to identify what to improve. Keep that optimisation work distinct from the acceptance checks for a correctly built first version.

title: Website Redesign Checklist: Preserve What Works
description: A redesign should improve the customer experience while preserving valuable URLs, content and integrations. Inventory the current website before deciding what to remove or rename.
subtitle: Website development guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: A redesign should improve the customer experience while preserving valuable URLs, content and integrations. Inventory the current website before deciding what to remove or rename.

sections.title: Record the baseline
body: Export the current sitemap and review important landing pages, search queries, backlinks and conversion paths. Save titles, canonicals and business-critical integrations. Use this inventory to distinguish a necessary change from a cosmetic preference.
bullets: Keep useful existing URLs when the page intent remains the same.
Map removed or replaced URLs to genuinely equivalent destinations.
Retain accurate content that helps customers decide.
Identify forms, payment flows and scripts that must survive the change.
Record performance and accessibility issues to verify after launch.

sections.title: Test the migration map
body: For each changed URL, check the intended permanent redirect and final successful destination. Avoid redirecting unrelated pages to the homepage just to eliminate a 404. Update internal links, canonicals and sitemap entries to the final URLs. Check that preview settings such as authentication or noindex do not leak into production.

sections.title: Launch with a recovery path
body: Use a reviewed preview, record the deployed version and keep a rollback option. Test contact and checkout flows on production, then inspect Search Console and analytics for unexpected changes. Some short-term variation is possible, so diagnose specific failures rather than reverting solely because one metric moved. A successful redesign keeps the business reachable and makes the important tasks easier to complete.

sections.title: Inventory what already earns its place
body: Before redesigning, list pages that receive search visits, enquiries or meaningful external links. Save their titles, content, URLs and conversion routes. Ask the business which pages customers actually mention. This gives the new design a set of responsibilities beyond looking different.

Identify weak content separately from weak presentation. A useful service explanation may need clearer formatting rather than deletion. A visually attractive page with vague information may need a rewrite. Keeping those diagnoses separate avoids rebuilding everything when a smaller change would solve the real problem.

sections.title: Map changed URLs one by one
body: When a page moves, choose a genuinely equivalent destination. Keep useful URLs where the intent remains the same. For removed content with no replacement, an appropriate not-found response can be more honest than redirecting every old link to the homepage.

Update links, canonical tags and sitemap entries to the final destinations. Test the redirect itself and the final response. A chain that eventually works can still be confusing to maintain. Keep the mapping as a review document so content decisions are visible before launch.

sections.title: Review the new site against the old business tasks
body: Use the same important journeys on the preview: reading a service, locating contact details, submitting an enquiry and completing any included purchase or booking. Check mobile behaviour, keyboard access and production integrations. Confirm that account ownership and verification methods survive the change.

After launch, watch specific evidence such as broken routes, missing enquiries and indexing changes. Record the deployment version and retain a recovery path. Search visibility can fluctuate while pages are recrawled, so investigate a reproducible problem rather than assuming every short-term movement means the redesign failed.

title: Landing Page Conversion Tracking Checklist
description: Set up landing-page conversion tracking around completed enquiries or purchases. Test event accuracy, duplicates, and reporting before launch.
subtitle: Website development guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Landing-page conversion tracking should distinguish a completed business action from a casual click. Define the event first, then test whether the implementation records it reliably.

sections.title: Write an event inventory
body: For each action, record its meaning, trigger, destination system and intended reporting use. Keep diagnostic interactions separate from primary conversion outcomes.
bullets: Form submitted successfully: verify server acceptance and delivery.
Call button clicked: label it as a click unless call completion is measured.
WhatsApp opened: do not describe this as a received or qualified enquiry.
Purchase completed: confirm transaction, value and currency.
Booking accepted: distinguish a booked appointment from opening the calendar.

sections.title: Use a practical test sheet
body: Test valid, invalid and repeated actions across mobile and desktop. Include consent choices, ad-blocking conditions where relevant and any handoff to another domain. In an illustrative form flow, a client-side success animation may appear while email delivery fails; the business record is an essential part of the check. Avoid placing names, phone numbers or email addresses in URLs and general analytics parameters.

sections.title: Maintain the measurement
body: Keep the event definition and test date with the page documentation. Retest after changes to forms, routing, analytics or consent handling. Compare reported conversions with unique business records and explain differences instead of treating every click as a customer. Reliable tracking improves decisions; it does not make attribution perfectly complete or remove the need to review lead quality.

sections.title: Distinguish intent from completion
body: Opening a contact form, pressing submit and receiving an accepted enquiry are three different events. A WhatsApp click opens a conversation route but does not establish that a message was sent. A calendar view does not establish that an appointment was booked. Name events so the report preserves those differences.

Choose the business system that confirms completion. For a form, that may be server acceptance and the configured delivery record; for a store, it is the confirmed order. Keep a labelled test record so the technical event can be compared with something the business actually received.

sections.title: Try the paths that should not create a conversion
body: Submit invalid input, press the button twice, refresh the confirmation screen and interrupt the connection. Inspect whether a success event appears when the action failed or whether one successful action is counted repeatedly. Test any handoff to a different domain as well.

Check the visitor’s relevant consent choices and reporting delays. A blocked measurement request is different from a failed enquiry. The page should still explain the business action accurately, and the report should not claim complete visibility when the measurement setup cannot provide it.

sections.title: Keep testing from becoming business performance
body: Label test enquiries clearly and document when testing took place. Use an agreed development or internal-traffic approach where appropriate. A report filter can hide a category from a view; it does not necessarily prevent collection. Active exclusion rules need careful validation because discarded future data may not be recoverable.

Review event counts alongside unique enquiries and sales records. Avoid sending names, phone numbers or message text as ordinary analytics parameters. Retest after changes to forms, routing, tags or consent settings, and record the exact success condition so the next developer does not accidentally replace it with a button-click event.

title: Website Speed Optimization Checklist
description: Find website speed bottlenecks with this checklist for images, fonts, scripts, and rendering. Measure real user journeys and verify improvements.
subtitle: Website development guides · ReddyStack · Updated 22 September 2026
intro: Improve website speed by finding the largest user-visible delays first. A performance score is useful diagnostic evidence, but it should not replace checking the actual customer journey.

sections.title: Measure before editing
body: Test representative pages on mobile and desktop. Distinguish lab results from real-user field data and record the conditions. Core Web Vitals cover loading, interaction responsiveness and visual stability; investigate the elements behind weak results rather than optimising only the score.
bullets: Images: correct dimensions, modern formats and lazy loading for below-the-fold content.
Main content: avoid making the key heading or image wait for unnecessary scripts.
Scripts: remove unused third-party work and defer nonessential features.
Fonts: reduce unnecessary files and check rendering behaviour.
Layout: reserve space for media and avoid unexpected shifts.

sections.title: Prioritise by impact
body: If a portfolio page downloads several multi-megabyte images, resizing and compressing those assets may matter more than a small stylesheet change. If the page appears quickly but freezes when a menu opens, inspect long-running work and interaction handling. Preserve image meaning and quality where customers need to inspect project details.

sections.title: Verify the complete flow
body: Repeat the same measurement after a meaningful change and test navigation, forms and animations. Confirm that performance edits did not hide content, break accessibility or remove necessary measurement. Keep the result and conditions in the change record. Set a practical asset budget for future uploads so the next content update does not immediately recreate the same loading problem.

sections.title: Read the metric behind the score
body: Largest Contentful Paint describes when the main visible content appears; Interaction to Next Paint describes responsiveness; Cumulative Layout Shift describes unexpected movement. Current good thresholds are LCP at or below 2.5 seconds, INP at or below 200 milliseconds and CLS at or below 0.1, assessed at the 75th percentile of real visits. A single lab run does not establish those field results.

Use lab tools to reproduce a problem and real-user data, when available, to understand the visitor experience. Keep device, connection and test conditions in the record. Comparing different pages under different conditions can make a small change look more important than it is.

sections.title: Fix the largest delay first
body: If the main image is too large, resize and compress it while preserving useful detail. If visible content waits for JavaScript, inspect that dependency. If the page becomes unresponsive during an interaction, investigate long-running work rather than spending the whole effort on image formats.

Review fonts and third-party scripts as part of the same page. Several small additions can create a large combined cost. Keep essential forms, accessibility and necessary measurement working while removing or deferring work that does not help the initial visit.

sections.title: Check the site after the optimisation
body: Repeat the same measurement and exercise navigation, forms, media and responsive layouts. A faster score is not a success if content remains hidden, a button stops working or text moves unexpectedly. Verify both the intended improvement and the journeys that depend on the changed code.

Set practical rules for future uploads: appropriate dimensions, compressed assets and a check before adding another tracking or animation script. Record what was measured rather than promising that one tool score will produce a ranking increase. Performance work should leave the website more usable and easier to maintain.

Keep a dated log of changes and review a long enough period for the traffic available. title: SEO and Local SEO guides
description: Practical seo and local seo guides from ReddyStack: checklists, planning examples and templates to help make better decisions.
subtitle: ReddyStack Insights
intro: Local search work starts with accurate business information and useful pages about the services you actually provide. This library covers website indexing, Google Business Profile, reviews, local listings and measurement. It explains the checks behind the work without promising a ranking position.

sections.title: Find out whether the problem is discovery or relevance
body: If a website is missing from Google, use the indexing and Search Console guides first. Check the exact URL, live availability, crawl access and canonical address. A page that cannot be indexed needs a different fix from a page that appears for relevant searches but earns few clicks.

For a visible site, the local SEO audit helps compare the actual service, location information, search result and enquiry page. Read the Business Profile guide before creating or changing a listing: eligibility and real-world business details matter, especially for businesses that visit customers.

sections.title: Build a maintenance routine you can sustain
body: Keep one record of approved business details, profile ownership and changes to hours or services. Use it when updating directories and your website. The citation guide focuses on useful, relevant listings; creating large numbers of poor listings is not a substitute for a helpful service page.

Ask real customers for honest reviews through a consistent process, then use the reporting guides to connect visibility with relevant enquiries. When traffic is small, compare longer periods and record the changes made. A few days of movement alone cannot establish whether an SEO change worked.

sections.title: What ReddyStack focuses on
body: The six core services are Meta Ads, Google Ads, Ad Creatives, AI UGC-Style Videos, Website Development, and SEO & Local SEO. Related work is grouped under these services so a business can discuss a clear outcome and scope. Apps, MVPs and automation remain additional work available on request.

sections.title: How I approach a project
body: I start with the business problem and the material already available. A business receiving unsuitable enquiries may need clearer service information before a larger advertising budget. A founder testing a product may need one working user journey before a long feature list. The brief should identify that first useful outcome.

Before work starts, the proposal should name the deliverables, review points, client inputs and exclusions. Missing copy, account access or product information can affect the plan, so those dependencies belong in the discussion. Platform charges and ongoing support should be visible as separate decisions.

sections.title: How to read the portfolio
body: The six projects on this website are personal or demo projects. They show development ideas and the decisions described on each page; they are not paid client case studies. ReddyStack has no client results to report at this stage.

You can assess the work by its structure, the user journey and the choices explained. The guides likewise use labelled examples to explain a calculation or workflow. An illustrative budget or conversion rate is not a promise about your campaign.

sections.title: What to send with an enquiry
body: Share your website or product link, what is currently difficult, the action you want customers to take and any deadline or budget boundary. A short description of the current process is usually more useful than a list of tools.

Keep passwords and private customer records out of the enquiry. If the project needs account access, the appropriate invitation and permissions can be agreed after the scope is clear. Your business should own the accounts and assets it depends on.
